1: Practical nine and ten: bivariate analysis in Python. In this lab we build a correlation matrix, heatmaps and cross tab analysis, and then generate hypotheses. We use the Superstore Retail Orders dataset, with sales, quantity, discount and profit, plus segment, category, region and ship mode.
2: Setup. We import pandas, numpy, seaborn and matplotlib. Then we read the C S V with the encoding set to latin one, which handles special characters in the file, and drop the rows where segment is missing, which removes a handful of blank trailing rows. Then df dot head shows the first rows.
3: Next we identify numerical and categorical features. The select dtypes function with include equals numpy number picks every numeric column in one command. We then drop postal code, because it is a number but it is an I D, not a measurement. So the numeric columns are sales, quantity, discount and profit. The categorical columns are ship mode, segment, region, category and sub category. These text columns have a manageable number of categories, so they are useful for cross tabs and boxplots. City, state and product name have hundreds of values, so we leave them out.
4: Covariance matrix for all numeric pairs at once. One command, df of numeric cols dot cov, computes covariance between every pair of the four features, with no loop. Notice the units. The covariance of sales and profit is about sixty nine thousand nine hundred eighty two, in dollars squared. The sign, positive, is meaningful, but the huge number itself is not comparable to the covariance of discount and profit, about minus ten point six. That is why we compute correlation next.
5: The correlation matrix, Pearson and Spearman. Df of numeric cols dot corr gives Pearson, the default, a linear correlation scaled from minus one to one. Adding method equals spearman gives the rank based version, which catches monotonic relationships and is robust to outliers. Sales and profit: plus point four eight by Pearson and point five two by Spearman, a moderate positive. Discount and profit: minus point two two by Pearson but minus point five four by Spearman, much stronger once ranked. Sales and quantity: weak positive. The jump for discount and profit happens because a few heavily discounted, deeply negative profit orders were flattening the straight line Pearson number.
6: The heatmap of the correlation matrix. We create a figure, then call seaborn's heatmap on the correlation matrix. Annot equals true prints each value on its cell, and vmin and vmax fix the colour scale to minus one to plus one, so intensity is always comparable. Look at the matrix: the diagonal is one, sales and profit are point four eight, and discount and profit are minus point two two.
7: Scatterplot and pairplot. One scatterplot shows one pair, here sales versus profit, and shows the shape a correlation number alone can hide. The pairplot, one command, draws a scatterplot for every pair of numeric features, with a histogram for each feature on the diagonal, covering all numeric pairs at once with no loop.
8: Now categorical with categorical: cross tabulation. Pandas crosstab of segment and ship mode counts how many orders fall into every combination. Adding normalize equals index turns each row into percentages, comparing the ship mode mix within each segment fairly. The result: all three segments cluster near fifty nine to sixty percent standard class, so shipping preference looks similar across segments.
9: A cross tab heatmap and a stacked bar chart. The heatmap uses the same shading idea as the numeric heatmap, applied to a cross tab instead of a correlation matrix. And calling dot plot with kind equals bar and stacked equals true directly on a cross tab turns counts into a stacked bar chart in one line, here showing the category mix by region.
10: Categorical with numerical: grouped statistics for every numeric feature at once. Df dot groupby category, then numeric cols, then mean, splits orders into three groups and averages all four numeric columns per group in one line, with no per feature loop. Using agg with mean and std gives both. Furniture has an average profit of about eight point seven dollars, office supplies twenty point three, and technology seventy eight point seven. Notice that technology has the highest average profit despite the lowest average discount.
11: Boxplots and a bar chart by category. The boxplot of profit by category shows the full distribution, median, spread and outliers, for each category. The bar plot with estimator equals mean shows average sales by segment, a simpler view comparing central tendency at a glance.
12: From findings to hypotheses. This is the most important step. Hypothesis one: discount hurts profit. The Spearman correlation is minus point five four, and it is strongest in the central region, where average discount is point two four versus point one one in the west. Hypothesis two: category drives profitability more than sales volume. Technology has the highest average profit despite a similar or lower sale size than furniture, which has the lowest. Hypothesis three: ship mode preference is independent of customer segment, since all three segments show about fifty nine to sixty percent standard class. Hypothesis four: regional discounting policy varies. Discount differs by region even though the category mix is nearly identical across regions, which suggests a policy effect, not a product mix effect. Remember, these are hypotheses generated by exploration, to be tested later on held out data.
13: A worked example on a second dataset, Titanic, with the same commands and new column names. We compute the correlation of age, fare, sibsp and parch, cross tab sex against survived with row percentages, group by passenger class, and draw a boxplot of fare by class. The cross tab reveals a well known finding: female passengers survived at a far higher rate than male passengers. And the groupby shows first class passengers paid a far higher average fare and were on average older. The same pattern works on any dataset.
14: Here is the lab code cheat sheet. For numerical with numerical: cov, corr, corr with method spearman, a seaborn heatmap, a scatterplot, and a pairplot. For categorical with categorical: pandas crosstab, with normalize equals index for row percentages, a heatmap of the cross tab, and a stacked bar plot. For categorical with numerical: groupby with mean, or agg with mean and std, a boxplot, and a bar plot with estimator mean. Keep this handy, and you can use it on the practical exam.
